kind.description: NARRATIVE is the argument: introduction, results and discussion, conclusion, and the abstract. GENERAL_METHODS is the experimental part's preface: instruments, solvents, purification, how spectra were recorded. PROCEDURE is how something was made or tried: one compound's preparation, the conditions screened for a reaction, a protocol that prepares no labelled compound. CHARACTERIZATION is one compound's data, including a comparison of the natural and the synthetic sample of it. CRYSTALLOGRAPHY is X-ray work -- crystal data, refinement, atomic coordinates, bond lengths and angles, displacement parameters -- which usually runs for pages and is one unit per structure, labelled with the compound crystallized. BIBLIOGRAPHY is the reference list, whatever the journal calls it and however it numbers it: where the author printed it as one run it is one unit from its first entry to its last, and where the journal prints the citations as numbered notes at the foot of each page, each run of consecutive citation blocks that stands between two units is a unit of its own; a run that falls inside a unit (between rows of one procedure, in the middle of a sentence) is not given, and that unit's range runs across it. What makes one of those notes part of it is that it cites a work -- authors, title, journal, year. A numbered note that instead says something about this work ("the two isomers were separated only once") is not a reference and is not BIBLIOGRAPHY, whatever number it carries. Do not read past the references for the document's chemistry unless there is a procedure printed after them, which does happen when a supplement is bound into the same file. OTHER is what none of these are: title and authors, affiliations, dates received, table of contents, acknowledgements, notes on the supporting information, and copies of spectra. A table of conditions screened for a reaction is not OTHER; it is PROCEDURE.
